C0.quote: we look at perpetual voting rules from an axiomatic perspective
C0.note: Perpetual voting rules aggregate approval ballots over a sequence of elections.

C1.quote: we fully characterize the axiomatic possibilities
C1.note: Mostly axiomatic. A few polynomial-time computability claims, e.g. Prop 8(v), so AL is minor.

C2.1.quote: An approval profile A = (A(1), . . . , A(n)) for C is an n-tuple of subsets

C2.2.quote: we assume that each voter v ∈ N approves some non-empty subset of C

C2.3.quote: Perpetual voting does not assume utility functions (but approval-based preferences)
C2.3.note: Preferences are mentioned but are identified with the approval sets.

C2.4.quote: subject to the preferences in Ak+1 and under consideration of H
C2.4.note: Approval profiles are treated as preferences and the rule is applied directly. No statement about reporting or sincerity.

C3.1.note: No analysis considers misreporting. Strategy-proofness is left as future work in Section 5.

C3.2.note: The related-work contrast says fairness should be achieved 'without strategic voting', but no statement that voters submit their held attitude.

C4.1.note: The paper uses 'satisfaction', defined as the number of rounds in which the winner is approved. That is a function of the input, not a utility concept, so the applicability condition is not met.

C4.2.note: The term dichotomous preferences is not used.

C5.1.note: Proportionality axioms such as ALQ, AUQ and the proportionality degree are presented as fairness to voters and groups. Satisfaction is also used.

C5.2.quote: the satisfaction of voter v ∈ N with w̄ is sat(v, w̄)
C5.2.note: Evaluation is on the approval input with no statement relating it to held attitudes.

VOT.note: Voters are inputs only and take no modelled action; strategic voting is not analysed.

CAN.note: Alternatives are only options to be chosen.

DES.note: The rule designer's choice is not modelled.

C7.1.note: Fewer than two types are present.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

claims.quote: Rotating Dictatorship offers an optimal dryspell guarantee of n, but is still an unacceptable rule
no committee member should be completely ignored
some rules that satisfy simple proportionality for technical reasons

C9.1.note: The paper makes claims about which rules are acceptable or proportional and about fairness towards voters.

C9.2.note: The claims about fairness towards voters and about which rules are acceptable need a statement that approval ballots equal voters' true approvals. This is not stated.

C10.1.note: The paper does not state a procedural reading.
